strengths: Rigorous experimental methodology with comprehensive ablations, multiple seeds, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and fair baseline comparisons using public implementations
Solid technical foundation with proper mathematical derivations and grounding in prior theoretical work on KL+entropy regularization
Practical significance: demonstrates 4-5x training efficiency gains over search-based methods with single-GPU training, improving reproducibility compared to AlphaZero
Thorough treatment of reproducibility: detailed implementation specifications, computational requirements, and use of public codebases (Pgx, Mctx)

Clear and honest presentation: authors transparently acknowledge that novelty lies primarily in the empirical result rather than algorithmic innovation, and clearly state focus on training efficiency versus asymptotic performance
Challenges conventional wisdom that search-based methods are necessary for board game playing, potentially inspiring future work on efficient model-free methods
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: KLENT combines three well-established techniques (KL regularization, entropy regularization, λ-returns) without introducing new algorithmic insights or theoretical contributions

Questionable evaluation metric: using simulator evaluations as efficiency measure conflates computational costs differently for model-free vs. search-based methods; while justified, this deserves deeper analysis of whether it fairly represents practical wall-clock training time

Weak scalability evidence: main results on medium-scale games; 19x19 Go results show only competitive (not superior) performance, suggesting model-free approach may not scale; limited analysis of why performance plateaus with larger board sizes

Convergence limitation: KLENT converges to quantal response equilibrium rather than Nash equilibrium; limited discussion of whether this suboptimal convergence is problematic or how test-time deterministic policies interact with this training convergence limit
Incomplete validation of applicability claims: paper claims applicability to theorem proving and combinatorial optimization but provides no experiments beyond board games
On-policy limitation reduces data efficiency: algorithm requires on-policy data collection; off-policy extension mentioned but not implemented or evaluated
Modest scope for ICML: results are specialized to board games domain and rely heavily on empirical validation rather than novel insights or broader theoretical contributions

strengths: Comprehensive and well-executed experimental evaluation across five board games with extensive ablation studies (Section 5.2) and sensitivity analyses (Appendix D) demonstrating all three components are necessary for performance

Strong reproducibility practices including detailed implementation details (Appendices B-C), multiple random seeds, validation of baseline implementations (Appendix F.2), and computational requirements documentation (Appendix K)
Significant practical efficiency gains: 4-5x improvement in simulator evaluations to reach comparable performance levels to AlphaZero (75M vs 300M evaluations to 50% win rate)
Clear mathematical framework with formal derivation of optimal policy (Appendix A) and convergence analysis on toy games (Appendix L) connecting to quantal response equilibrium
Well-organized presentation with clear motivation, good problem formulation, and helpful visualizations of core concepts (Figure 2 comparison, Figure 3-4 analysis)
weaknesses: Severely limited algorithmic novelty: combines three well-established techniques (KL regularization from Sokota et al. 2022, entropy regularization from Perolat et al. 2021, λ-returns from Sutton 1988) with only one modification (analytical policy as learning target). Authors explicitly acknowledge: 'the novelty of this study lies in our empirical result' rather than methodological innovation

Questionable efficiency metrics and unfair comparisons: (1) 'Simulator evaluations' metric doesn't capture full computational cost including MCTS overhead, (2) no wall-clock training time in main results despite parallel execution across 1024 threads, (3) Appendix H shows test-time search substantially narrows gap, suggesting efficiency gains are partly methodological artifacts, (4) DQN/PPO baselines use Stable-Baselines3 defaults without domain-specific tuning

Asymptotic performance concerns undermine practical significance: paper acknowledges 'does not necessarily mean superior asymptotic performance when unlimited computational resources are given'; Appendix G.3 Table 6 shows AlphaZero reaches 89% at 3,200M-4,000M evaluations versus KLENT's 89% at 800M, and efficiency advantage evaporates for practitioners with sufficient resources

Severe hyperparameter sensitivity and poor generalization: unified hyperparameters (α=0.03, β=0.1, λ=e^{-1/8}) across diverse games despite Appendix D showing dramatic performance drops (29% vs 76% in 9x9 Go with suboptimal values); no principled methodology for hyperparameter selection on new domains, raising robustness questions

Insufficient justification for core design decisions: (1) claims action-value learning is harder but λ-returns proposed as solution without explaining why this specific technique addresses action-conditional variation challenges, (2) bias-variance analysis (Figure 4) uses only pretrained model, not learning dynamics, (3) on-policy limitation inherently less sample-efficient than off-policy methods, mentioned but not adequately discussed or explored (Retrace(λ) variant unexamined)

Limited scope and generalization: only five board games with finite action spaces and perfect information tested; claims about applicability to 'discrete optimization, algorithmic discovery, mathematical proving' are speculative; no evidence method works beyond this narrow domain class

Weak theoretical contribution: Appendix A provides standard Lagrangian optimization (not novel), Appendix L convergence analysis on toy count-up game doesn't generalize to complex games; no theoretical guarantees or insights into why combination works

Baseline comparison issues: original AlphaZero unavailable so Pgx implementation used; limited comparison with recent efficient methods (no MuZero comparison); DQN and PPO hyperparameters may not be domain-optimized

Incomplete analysis of design choices: paper doesn't explore why direct action-value modeling is better than alternatives, whether learning both V and Q like AlphaZero would work, or provide principled guidance for practitioners on hyperparameter selection for new games

strengths: Addresses a significant practical problem: the 10+ GPU-year training cost of AlphaZero is a real reproducibility barrier, and demonstrating 4x efficiency gains is valuable for democratizing research in this domain.

Comprehensive experimental validation across five diverse board games with systematic ablation studies clearly demonstrating that all three components (KL regularization, entropy regularization, λ-returns) are essential for performance.

Exceptional reproducibility and transparency: detailed experimental setup, wall-clock time analysis, verification of baseline implementations against alternative repositories, and documented computational costs (~2000 GPU hours).

Strong and consistent empirical results: efficient learning across multiple domains with proper statistical reporting (multiple seeds, error bands), sensitivity analysis on hyperparameters, and head-to-head validation against established baselines (Pachi, GnuGo).

Honest treatment of limitations and scope: authors clearly articulate that their focus is training efficiency (not asymptotic performance), acknowledge potential superiority of search-based methods with unlimited resources, and properly discuss convergence to quantal response equilibrium.

Technically sound theoretical framework: the closed-form solution derivation (Theorem A.2) is elegant, bias-variance tradeoff analysis for λ-returns is well-motivated, and convergence limit analysis (Appendix L) provides good theoretical grounding.

Challenges important assumption: demonstrates that model-free approaches can be competitive with search-based methods in a domain where search has dominated for decades, opening new research directions for resource-efficient RL.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the three core techniques (KL regularization, entropy regularization, λ-returns) all exist in prior work. The primary contribution is empirical demonstration that their combination works well for board games, rather than novel methodology. Authors acknowledge this by stating 'novelty lies in empirical result,' which is somewhat weak for a top-tier venue.

Function approximator mismatch confounds efficiency comparison: KLENT learns Q(s,a) while AlphaZero learns V(s), which have fundamentally different expressiveness and learning difficulty. While justified, this makes direct efficiency comparison less clean and raises questions about whether results are due to algorithmic superiority or function class choices.

Incomplete scalability analysis: (1) 19×19 Go results show KLENT plateaus at ~40-50% win rate while asymptotic performance of AlphaZero remains unclear; (2) extended budget experiments (Table 6) only reach 4.8B evaluations; (3) no clear demonstration that KLENT scales to the largest problems where AlphaZero excels.

Efficiency metric ambiguity: 'simulator evaluations' treats search-based and model-free methods differently (samples/rollouts vs. raw samples). While wall-clock time analysis in appendices partially addresses this, the main narrative uses a metric that may inherently favor model-free methods. Primary efficiency claims should more clearly establish wall-clock time improvements.

Limited theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, or approximation error analysis. The convergence to quantal response equilibrium (Appendix L) rather than Nash equilibrium is a fundamental limitation that deserves more prominent discussion in the main paper.

Hyperparameter tuning questions: while unified hyperparameters across five games is impressive, the paper doesn't clearly establish that baselines were equally well-tuned per-game. Sensitivity analysis (Appendix D) is only on 9×9 Go, leaving questions about generalization of the chosen hyperparameter values.

On-policy limitation not adequately addressed: the algorithm requires on-policy self-play data collection. Authors mention extending to off-policy via Retrace(λ) but don't implement or test this, limiting practical applicability and preventing comparison with off-policy alternatives.

Statistical rigor could be strengthened: while error bands are shown, only 3 random seeds are used (more would strengthen claims) and no formal significance testing is provided. Claims about 'several-fold efficiency gains' would benefit from confidence intervals.

strengths: Strong empirical results with consistent 4x efficiency gains across five diverse board games, demonstrating practical value
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple strong baselines, thorough ablation studies, and extensive robustness checks in appendices

Novel theoretical contributions: Theorem 5.1 improves convergence conditions over prior work (Sokota et al. 2022); Theorem 5.2 establishes convergence for finite-length games via backward induction with rigorous proofs
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, network architectures, implementation details, and sensitivity analyses enabling independent validation
Honest treatment of limitations and contribution scope; candid discussion of theory-practice gaps and domain restrictions
Well-designed experiments with appropriate metrics (simulator evaluations) fairly comparing training efficiency across methods
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of problem motivation and theoretical/empirical results
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: combines three well-established techniques (reverse-KL, entropy regularization, λ-returns) without deep explanation of synergistic effects; contribution is primarily empirical validation of the combination

Significant theory-practice gap: normal-form game analysis assumes static payoff matrices; finite-length game convergence assumes perfect value estimates; both ignore function approximation and self-play non-stationarity present in real games

Incomplete justification for design choices: (1) λ-returns validation uses frozen networks, unclear if optimal during training; (2) Q(s,a) vs. V(s) modeling choice not justified theoretically or empirically against AlphaZero's approach; (3) universal hyperparameters (α, β, λ) work across games but lack principled selection method

Hyperparameter robustness concerning: sensitivity analysis (Appendix G) shows 20-92% win rate variation across hyperparameter settings; apparent universality across games may be fortunate rather than principled, limiting confidence in generalization

Self-play dynamics not addressed: theoretical results assume fixed or adversarially-improving opponents via backward induction, but convergence properties under actual non-stationary self-play are uncharacterized
Local convergence only: Theorem 5.1 provides local linear convergence in unspecified neighborhood; global convergence properties and practical convergence rates remain unknown

Limited scope: restricted to two-player zero-sum games with finite-action spaces; deterministic transitions; extensions to continuous actions and stochastic environments are mentioned but not validated

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 board games with thorough ablation studies demonstrating importance of each component
Technically sound theoretical analysis with correct proofs using spectral radius methods and backward induction
Honest discussion of limitations explicitly acknowledging lack of asymptotic performance advantage, only efficiency gains
Well-presented paper with clear motivation and extensive supplementary materials
Reasonable practical algorithm combining existing techniques effectively for resource-constrained settings
weaknesses: Severely limited algorithmic novelty: combines well-known techniques (reverse-KL + entropy regularization + λ-returns) with minimal innovation; authors explicitly acknowledge contributions are 'characterizations' not new methods
Incremental theoretical contributions: Theorem 5.1 only modestly improves Sokota et al. (2022); Theorem C.12 is straightforward backward induction following expected RL theory

Unfair experimental comparisons: efficiency metric (simulator evaluations) conflates algorithmic differences with implementation costs; AlphaZero includes expensive MCTS per evaluation while KLENT counts only environment steps; Appendix L.3 shows AlphaZero reaches same performance with higher budget, expected due to search overhead

Misleading framing: paper presents eliminating search as an algorithmic advantage when search is necessary for AlphaZero's design; lacks wall-clock training time comparison accounting for MCTS overhead

Severely limited scope: only 5 board games tested; claims about discrete optimization and algorithmic discovery unvalidated; on low-branching-factor games (Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess) KLENT is merely competitive
Suspicious baseline performance: Discrete SAC and V-MPO achieve <1% win rate (Appendix J), raising fairness-of-comparison concerns
Theory-practice gap: convergence theorems assume exact policy updates; Algorithm 1 uses neural network function approximation without analysis of approximation error
Limited evaluation protocol: uses fixed anchored opponent rather than full self-play convergence; doesn't validate claims about generalization to other domains

strengths: Clear motivation addressing important gap: can model-free RL match AlphaZero efficiency without search?
Solid theoretical contributions improving upon Sokota et al. (2022) with broader convergence region; convergence guarantees for finite-length games verified empirically
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 diverse board games plus 19x19 Go with extensive ablations validating each component (KL, entropy, λ-returns)
Rigorous methodology with unified network architecture across all methods, multiple random seeds, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and test-time evaluation comparisons
Practical algorithm with demonstrated efficiency: 4× improvement (300M→75M evaluations for 50% win rate) with simple, reproducible approach
Honest and thorough limitations discussion: acknowledges limited algorithmic novelty, local theoretical convergence, and focus on training rather than asymptotic efficiency
Exceptional thoroughness with 31-page appendices including architecture comparisons, implementation details, sensitivity analysis, and additional validations on Count Up Game
Elegant closed-form optimal policy solution (Eq. 3) enabling efficient model-free learning by directly modeling action-value functions without MCTS
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: reverse KL + entropy combination is known from existing literature; contributions characterized as 'characterizations' rather than novel ingredients, limiting impact despite solid execution

Theoretical results are local (require proximity to Nash equilibrium) and incremental: Theorem 5.1 improves Sokota et al. bound but uses standard Jacobian spectral radius analysis; gap between normal-form game theory and neural network practice

Scope limitations: experiments limited to deterministic environments with finite action spaces; claimed applicability to stochastic settings and 'real-world applications' (discrete optimization, algorithm discovery) not validated; mostly 9×9 Go rather than larger scales

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: paper lacks explanation of why reverse KL + entropy outperforms alternatives (DQN, PPO, SAC, V-MPO all fail dramatically); why this specific combination stabilizes self-play is not analyzed

Experimental concerns: different network architectures across methods (KLENT uses action-value head, AlphaZero uses state-value), single baseline opponent for evaluation, hyperparameter robustness questioned by Appendix G sensitivity (α=0.01, β=0.03 fails), evaluation methodology choices (reactive policy) may bias results

Large test-time performance gap (Figure 15): KLENT without search substantially underperforms Gumbel AlphaZero, raising questions about learned representation quality and practical deployment; limited discussion of implications

Finite-horizon theoretical assumption: Theorem C.12 proof relies on bounded Tmax and backward induction; does not extend to infinite-horizon discounted settings (acknowledged in C.14), limiting theoretical generality

Missing justifications: choice of λ=e^(-1/8) from single preliminary experiment (Figure 2), no theoretical guidance for hyperparameters α and β, O(|A|) softmax computation scalability to large action spaces unclear
